narrative:
“Shelter,” you say. The word comes readily; what follows does not. “That’s what I was taught.”

Lio looks toward the window, then back at you. “For somebody inside, or somebody trying to get in?”

You have opened that volume every winter to check the dates of the memorial observances. You know the mark on its cover better than the names beneath it. Now you cannot remember whether any page actually calls it shelter.

“There’s a book downstairs,” you tell him. “We’ll look before we touch that door.”

He releases a breath through his nose. “Good.” Then, with a glance at the bench: “Can we leave that here?”

You set a shallow metal tray beneath the rope without lifting it. Water ticks onto the tin. The coil lies still, its cut end pale and fibrous, ordinary enough to make the trickle worse. You leave the lamp burning beside it and lead Lio down the spiral stairs. He follows close, keeping the towel between his hands and the rail.

The archive occupies a cramped room above the entrance passage. *Cold paper, lamp oil, the dry bitterness of mouse-chewed paste.* Dawn presses faintly against its single window. You light the desk lamp and kneel before the lowest shelf, where the oldest books sit on wooden battens above the damp. Your knees make the familiar small protests. Lio crouches beside you without being asked and takes the weight of the volume when you ease it free.

“Flat on the desk,” you say.

“I know. My grandmother’s prayer book comes apart if you breathe wrong.”

His attempt at a smile almost succeeds.

The branching impression in the leather is shallow. Under lamplight, with the book turned sideways, it resembles three passages meeting at a narrow entrance. You trace beside it with your sound fingers, careful not to touch the brittle surface, then open to the founding account.

You read aloud. “On the ninth day, those received above the flood were entered by household and vessel.”

“Above,” Lio repeats.

The next page lists donations: bronze, timber, meal, lamp oil. You turn it. Near the gutter, a line has been crowded beneath the formal text in smaller lettering. You bring the lamp closer.

“‘The lower entrance shall remain answerable to the keeper.’”

Lio’s towel stops moving between his hands.

You remember your mentor making you carry lamp oil up from the entrance passage, one tin in each hand. You remember him insisting that a keeper must always know who stood outside before drawing a bolt. You had taken it for ordinary caution, the instruction of a man who had once admitted a drunken stranger and lost three teeth for it.

Here, beneath the cramped line, someone has drawn the branching mark again.

**One branch ends in a tiny open square. The other two end in bars.**

“Does answerable mean you have to open it?” Lio asks.

“No.” You study the lettering until your eyes begin to water. “It means I can’t pretend nobody knocked.”

A soft scrape comes from the entrance passage.

You raise your head. Lio rises first, taking a step toward the archive doorway, then checks himself and looks at you. You lift the lamp and follow him as far as the threshold.

Below, the lighthouse’s outer door remains shut. Beneath it, a thin tongue of water advances across the flagstones, carrying a single strand of dark weed. It moves against the slope of the floor. You know that slope: every winter you sweep rainwater down it and out.

Three taps sound from the small iron hatch beside the stair foot, the hatch you use to reach the old drainage channel.

Lio draws back until his shoulder touches the doorframe. “That goes under the cliff, doesn’t it?”

“Yes.”

Something shifts behind the iron. Then a voice reaches you, blurred by the narrow passage but plainly human.

“Keeper. Is the upper door still open to households?”

Your hand tightens on the lamp handle. The question belongs to the page lying open behind you. At the stair foot, water gathers around the hatch’s lower hinge.

Lio catches your sleeve lightly. “Ask how many,” he whispers. “Before you promise anything.”

quick_actions.text: Secure the outer door and watch the rising water
Descend and open the drainage hatch
Ask the unseen visitor who needs shelter

scene_description: *A cramped coastal lighthouse archive before dawn, lit by a warm oil lamp.* A broad, stooped 58-year-old brown-skinned man with close-cropped silver hair, hazel eyes, a pale burn scar across his left cheek, and two shortened right fingers stands at the archive doorway holding the lamp. He wears heavy dark wool workwear and sturdy leather boots, his expression tense and attentive. Beside him, a slight 19-year-old deep-brown-skinned man with tightly curled hair and a white streak above his right temple grips his sleeve; he wears a patched oversized fisherman’s sweater, wet trousers, and flexible boots, with a towel clutched in his other hand. Behind them an ancient leather book lies open on a wooden desk. A narrow stone staircase descends to a closed outer door and a small iron drainage hatch; a thin stream of seawater crosses the flagstones toward the hatch. **Warm lamplight contrasts with cold blue dawn and damp stone.**

summary_update.current_situation: Ajax and Lio stand at the eastern lighthouse archive doorway overlooking the entrance passage. An unseen voice behind the drainage hatch asks whether the upper door still admits households; seawater is moving uphill across the floor. The oldest archive volume lies open with a clause making the keeper answerable for the lower entrance. Ajax must decide how to respond.

character_updates.current_state: At the archive doorway in the eastern lighthouse before dawn, holding an oil lamp, physically unharmed and unsettled. Has found a founding clause requiring the lower entrance to remain answerable to the keeper. Faces an unseen visitor speaking through the drainage hatch while seawater moves uphill into the entrance passage; has made no promise of admission.

Beside Ajax at the archive doorway, frightened but thinking practically, lightly holding Ajax's sleeve and carrying a towel. His trousers remain wet and his wrist is free. Urges Ajax to ask how many visitors need shelter before promising admission. His strange rope remains in a metal tray in the lantern room.

Seawater enters the lighthouse against the floor's slope, and an unseen voice behind the drainage hatch asks whether households can still receive shelter above.
